name: Complex-step first derivative
definition: For real x and nonzero real h, D_h f(x)=Im(f(x+ih))/h. If f is holomorphic near x and real on the real axis, D_h f(x)=f′(x)−h²f‴(x)/6+O(h⁴) as h→0 in exact arithmetic.
variables: x real evaluation point; i imaginary unit; h real nonzero step; Im imaginary part; f′ and f‴ first and third derivatives
assumptions: A holomorphic extension on a neighborhood containing the perturbed point, real values on the real axis, and an evaluation that preserves the small imaginary perturbation without unrelated imaginary rounding noise
limitations: No subtraction of two nearly equal real outputs is needed, but underflow, imaginary noise, nonanalytic operations and complex-unsafe implementations can still invalidate the approximation
failure_conditions: Nonfinite output, underflow of the perturbation or unsupported complex arithmetic
Nonanalytic operations or known loss of the imaginary component
computation: Evaluate f at x+ih within the analytic neighborhood; divide its imaginary part by h. Inspect the evaluation path for real-only casts, conjugation, absolute values or unrelated imaginary noise; compare estimates across representable steps where feasible. Agreement alone is not an error certificate; report unresolved numerical behavior rather than assuming arbitrary small h is safe.

source.citation: Higham, N. J. (2018), Differentiation With(out) a Difference, SIAM News 51(5), equation (1) and discussion of imaginary rounding, https://www.siam.org/publications/siam-news/articles/differentiation-without-a-difference ; signed Taylor correction independently derived.

required_inputs: Analytic complex-safe function, real point, representable nonzero step and a neighborhood where analyticity holds
incompatible_methods: Nonanalytic absolute value or imaginary-component suppression
mechanism_note: Complex perturbation obtains the derivative from the imaginary component rather than differences of real outputs. Related to first difference, but a distinct derivative approximation.

name: Finite-difference weights by moment matching
definition: For n≥2 distinct real offsets s_j=h t_j with h>0 and integer 1≤m<n, solve Σ_(j=0)^(n−1) c_j t_j^k=m! δ_(km) for k=0,…,n−1. Set w_j=c_j/h^m and D_m f(x)=Σ_j w_j f(x+s_j). This is exact on polynomials of degree at most n−1.
variables: n node count; m derivative order; h positive scale; t_j distinct dimensionless offsets; s_j physical offsets; c_j scaled weights; w_j derivative weights; δ Kronecker delta
assumptions: Distinct real nodes, finite samples, and sufficient smoothness on the interval containing x and all nodes; for fixed distinct t_j and f with bounded nth derivative the Taylor error is O(h^(n−m)) as h tends to zero
limitations: The Vandermonde moment system and weighted summation may be ill-conditioned; scaling does not guarantee stability; noise grows with derivative order and inverse step scale
failure_conditions: Duplicate or collapsed nodes, nonfinite samples or weights
Unresolved moment system conditioning or numerical residual within the chosen precision
computation: Scale offsets by a positive h, construct V_(kj)=t_j^k with k=0,…,n−1 and right side m!δ_(km). Solve Vc=b with a suitable pivoted solver, assess conditioning and residual, then sum the weighted samples with h^(−m) scaling. Reject unresolved numerical solves; a small residual alone cannot certify the derivative error.

source.citation: Driscoll, T. A. and Braun, R. J., Fundamentals of Numerical Computation, §5.4 Finite differences, https://tobydriscoll.net/fnc-julia/localapprox/finitediffs.html ; Persson, P.-O., UC Berkeley Math 128A, §4.1, https://persson.berkeley.edu/math128a/lecture_notes/math128a_lecture_notes_chapter_4.html ; arbitrary-node, arbitrary-order moment equations and error order independently derived from polynomial exactness and Taylor expansion.

required_inputs: Finite function samples at n distinct real offsets, positive scaling factor, integer derivative order and a numerical solve tolerance/precision policy
mechanism_note: Derivative functional of the same unique interpolating polynomial rather than a new polynomial approximation family. A derivative-output variant of polynomial interpolation; direct moment solving is not Fornberg recursion and ordinary difference stencils are special cases.
